Goldman’s Risk Appetite Indicator* which made a lot of headlines the prior week falling to the least since April 2025 rebounded to −0.3 from −0.5, snapping a four-week losing streak, and the momentum index edged up to −0.8 from −0.9.

Under the hood, credit remains the weak spot. Its sub-component bounced to −2.0, but the prior week it fell to about −3, well below its April 2025 low (around −1.8) and the lowest since at least the start of 2025 (where the chart begins). Equities recovered to around flat (−0.1). 

Goldman’s asset allocation team adds that cross-asset sentiment and positioning “are back to more neutral levels,” and its equity tail-risk model “still points to a less negative asymmetry… but with worsening signal from the business cycle and sentiment.”

*"Goldman Sachs Risk Appetite Indicator (RAI) aims to track the level of global market risk appetite and risk aversion based on various market variables. A sharp rise in the index can send a warning signal that investors have more risk appetite and are potentially exposed to a correction if consensus views are tested. Similarly, a sharp decline indicates a reduction in risk appetite, and at extreme levels it can indicate that markets may have overshot. RAI signals are most powerful when the level of risk appetite is very low below -1.5, with levels closer to -2.0 giving the clearest signal over longer time horizons, as at such levels the asymmetry of subsequent medium term equity return becomes very positively skewed. RAI momentum is designed to track short term shifts of market risk appetite, and subcomponents of the RAI.”

"People who take a ton of stimulants and just blitz, blitz, blitz, blitz, blitz. These are the same people that crash and disappear. You have to figure out and build your capacity."

💸🗳️Affordability will be one of the biggest issues on voters’ minds today.

And while we wait for the vote counts to start coming in, our colleagues at @economics just released a fascinating new way to look at it: the Bloomberg Price Project.

It uses millions of alternative-data price points to break inflation down into nearly 700 categories — more than 3x the detail of the official CPI.

And maybe best of all, the full dataset is available to all Bloomberg Terminal clients via ECAN US BPI <GO>.

The big picture: inflation is still too high, but the pressure looks much less broad-based than it did in 2022. A relatively narrow group of categories — particularly energy and AI-exposed goods — is doing much of the heavy lifting.

And at least one bit of relief at the grocery store: the surge in beef prices appears to be reversing. 🥩📉

A very cool dataset to explore — read more about it here, and dig deeper on ECAN US BPI <GO>: 
https://t.co/yy7FfxjswX
